title: Future Continuous, Future Perfect and Future Perfect Continuous
summary: Distinguish future activities in progress, events completed before a future deadline and activities continuing up to a future point. Use the future continuous for regular future events and neutral questions about arrangements, and recognise advanced inference uses of these future forms.
learningObjectives: Describe an activity expected to be in progress at a specified future moment and a future event that is part of an ordinary routine.
Ask tactful, neutral questions about future arrangements using will be + -ing rather than presenting the question as a request.
Choose future perfect for completion or achievement and future perfect continuous to emphasise duration up to a future reference point.
Interpret future forms as inferences about what is probably happening now or what has probably been happening until now.

explanation.heading: Future continuous: activity underway at a future point
explanation.body: Will be + -ing locates an activity in progress at a future moment. The activity may have started earlier and may continue afterwards; the form does not itself promise that the activity will be finished. The future continuous can also describe something expected in the normal course of a routine or programme, without highlighting a decision at the moment of speaking.
explanation.example: When the visitors reach the atrium at eleven, the musicians will be rehearsing on the upper floor.

explanation.heading: Scheduled events and tactful questions with will be doing
explanation.body: We can describe planned or habitual future activities with the future continuous. Compared with a question using plain will, Will you be ...? is often a neutral enquiry about someone’s existing arrangements rather than a request, an invitation or a test of willingness. Both a future continuous and a present continuous may fit a settled plan; the speaker’s communicative purpose decides which sounds better.
explanation.example: Will you be working in the reading room tomorrow afternoon? I need to know whether the desk will be occupied.

explanation.heading: Future perfect: completed before a reference point
explanation.body: Will have + past participle presents an event as completed or a target as achieved by a future deadline. The future reference point is often expressed by by, before or by the time, and it can also be understood from context. A passive future perfect uses will have been + past participle. The future perfect can also make courteous predictions about how a previous message will have been received.
explanation.example: By the time the exhibition opens, the team will have installed every display. All the labels will have been checked.

explanation.heading: Future perfect continuous: looking back at duration
explanation.body: Will have been + -ing stresses the length or continuity of an activity leading up to a future point. The activity may still be under way at that point. The future perfect simple can sometimes also express duration, especially with long-standing situations, but the continuous foregrounds ongoing effort or repeated activity rather than a completed product or count.
explanation.example: At the end of this term, Leila will have been teaching at the college for twelve years.

explanation.heading: Inferences about now and recent past
explanation.body: Future continuous can express an assumption about what is happening around now, not only literal future time. Similarly, future perfect can refer to something assumed to have happened by now; future perfect continuous can suggest the length of an activity up to a past or present reference point, often from the speaker’s perspective now. These inferential uses need context, and they should not be confused with definite knowledge.
explanation.example: Do not call the manager during the ceremony; she will be speaking to the guests. The invitations will have reached everyone by now.

comparisons.title: An activity in progress versus a completed result

left.label: Future continuous: in progress
left.example: At nine tomorrow, I will be editing the catalogue.
left.note: The editing is expected to be underway at nine; no completion is asserted.

right.label: Future perfect: complete by then
right.example: By nine tomorrow, I will have edited the catalogue.
right.note: The editing is expected to be finished by nine.

comparisons.title: Future perfect result versus future perfect continuous duration

left.label: Future perfect: completed quantity
left.example: By Friday, we will have tested forty samples.
left.note: Attention falls on the number of tests completed.

right.label: Future perfect continuous: duration
right.example: By Friday, we will have been testing samples for two weeks.
right.note: Attention falls on how long the testing activity has continued.

examples.sentence: This time tomorrow, the interview panel will be examining the shortlisted candidates.
examples.note: The future continuous places an ongoing activity at a later time.

examples.sentence: Will you be bringing your laptop to the workshop, or should we arrange one?
examples.note: Will you be bringing enquires neutrally about an existing intention.

examples.sentence: By the end of the month, the engineers will have updated all the safety notices.
examples.note: The future perfect signals completion before a deadline.

examples.sentence: In September, the volunteers will have been restoring the garden for three full years.
examples.note: The future perfect continuous looks back at an ongoing period from a future point.

examples.sentence: She will have heard about the timetable change by now, so another message may be unnecessary.
examples.note: Will have heard is an inference about an event assumed to have already occurred.

commonMistakes.incorrect: At six tomorrow, I will working on the budget.
commonMistakes.correct: At six tomorrow, I will be working on the budget.
commonMistakes.why: Future continuous requires will be followed by an -ing form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: By next Tuesday, they will have prepare the room.
commonMistakes.correct: By next Tuesday, they will have prepared the room.
commonMistakes.why: Future perfect requires the past participle after will have.

commonMistakes.incorrect: By January, we will have been collect data for two years.
commonMistakes.correct: By January, we will have been collecting data for two years.
commonMistakes.why: Future perfect continuous is built with will have been plus an -ing verb.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Will you be use the projector during the morning session?
commonMistakes.correct: Will you be using the projector during the morning session?
commonMistakes.why: A neutral question about existing arrangements uses will + subject + be + -ing.

studyTips: Draw a timeline for at, by and for: mark what will be happening, what will be finished and how long an activity will have lasted.
Practise neutral questions about colleagues’ existing plans using Will you be ...? and compare their effect with direct Will you ...? questions.
For every perfect-continuous example, name its reference point and duration; for every perfect example, name the result expected to be complete.

exercises.prompt: When you ring at eleven tomorrow, I ___ a training session, so I probably cannot answer immediately.
choices: will be leading
will have led
led
exercises.feedback: Will be leading describes the activity underway at the future time of the call.

exercises.prompt: Which question neutrally enquires about an existing plan, rather than sounding like a request to do something?
choices: Do you using the main hall after lunch?
Will you be using the main hall after lunch?
Will you been using the main hall after lunch?
exercises.feedback: Will you be using is the correct future continuous question and conventionally asks about a future arrangement.

exercises.prompt: The archive has a strict deadline: by midday Friday, the team ___ all six boxes of documents.
choices: will cataloguing
will be catalogued
will have catalogued
exercises.feedback: Will have catalogued presents all six boxes as fully processed by the deadline.

exercises.prompt: Which form explicitly stresses the duration of a continuing activity up to a future point?
choices: will have been coordinating
will coordinate
will be coordinating
exercises.feedback: Will have been coordinating focuses on how long the activity has lasted up to the future reference point.

exercises.prompt: At three tomorrow afternoon, the curators ___ (examine) the paintings. Write the complete future continuous verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Will be examining places an unfinished activity at a particular future time.

exercises.prompt: By the time the guests arrive, the caterers ___ (prepare) every table. Write the complete future perfect verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Will have prepared marks completed work by the guests’ arrival.

exercises.prompt: By next April, Nadia ___ (work) on this programme for eight years. Write the complete future perfect continuous verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Will have been working emphasises the period of activity leading up to next April.

exercises.prompt: Our usual schedule continues tomorrow: we ___ (meet) the regional coordinators after breakfast. Use future continuous.
exercises.feedback: Will be meeting describes an anticipated event in the normal course of the programme.

exercises.prompt: Correct the verb phrase: “When the workshop starts, we will be discuss the new policy.”
acceptedAnswers: When the workshop starts, we will be discussing the new policy.
exercises.feedback: After will be, use the -ing form discussing.

exercises.prompt: Correct the future perfect: “By Thursday, the editor will have proofreaded the manuscript.”
acceptedAnswers: By Thursday, the editor will have proofread the manuscript.
exercises.feedback: The past participle of proofread is proofread, not proofreaded.

exercises.prompt: Correct the duration form: “By winter, she will have been teach at this school for a decade.”
acceptedAnswers: By winter, she will have been teaching at this school for a decade.
exercises.feedback: Future perfect continuous requires will have been teaching.

exercises.prompt: Correct this neutral question: “Will you be attend the research briefing on Monday?”
acceptedAnswers: Will you be attending the research briefing on Monday?
exercises.feedback: Future continuous questions use will + subject + be + present participle.

speakingExercises.prompt: At ten tomorrow, the team / analyse / the results. Express an activity in progress using future continuous and full forms.
acceptedAnswers: At ten tomorrow, the team will be analysing the results.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will be analysing frames the activity as underway at a future moment.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask neutrally about a plan using the exact facts: you / use / the library desk / tomorrow morning. Begin with “Will” and use future continuous.
acceptedAnswers: Will you be using the library desk tomorrow morning?
speakingExercises.feedback: Will you be using asks about an existing arrangement without making a direct request.

speakingExercises.prompt: The deadline is Friday. Facts: By Friday / the organiser / send / every invitation. Use the future perfect.
acceptedAnswers: By Friday, the organiser will have sent every invitation.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will have sent describes completion before Friday.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe how long work will continue. Facts: By July / they / work / on the renovation / for six months. Use future perfect continuous.
acceptedAnswers: By July, they will have been working on the renovation for six months.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will have been working focuses on the accumulated duration.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a present-time inference. Facts: The director / speak / to the visitors / now. Use future continuous and start with “The director”.
acceptedAnswers: The director will be speaking to the visitors now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will be speaking can express an assumption about an ongoing present activity.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a future perfect passive statement. Facts: By Monday / the invitations / deliver. Use full forms.
acceptedAnswers: By Monday, the invitations will have been delivered.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will have been delivered is the passive future perfect for completion.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the grammar aloud: “By December, I will have been study this subject for three years.”
acceptedAnswers: By December, I will have been studying this subject for three years.
speakingExercises.feedback: After will have been, use the -ing form studying.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two sentences in this order, using full forms. Activity at nine: We / rehearse / at nine tomorrow. Completion by noon: We / finish / by noon tomorrow.
acceptedAnswers: We will be rehearsing at nine tomorrow. We will have finished by noon tomorrow.
speakingExercises.feedback: Future continuous describes a point during rehearsal; future perfect describes completion by noon.

listeningExercises.audioText: When you arrive at the workshop at half past two, the participants will be discussing the second proposal. The meeting will still be in progress.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker expect at half past two?
choices: A discussion already finished before lunch.
An ongoing discussion of the second proposal.
A workshop scheduled for next month.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will be discussing presents an activity still underway at the stated time.

listeningExercises.audioText: Will you be driving to the community centre this evening? I only want to know whether the parking space will be free.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker ask about driving?
choices: To order the listener to drive.
To offer driving lessons.
To find out about an existing plan and parking availability.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will you be driving enquires about arrangements and the reason is parking availability.

listeningExercises.audioText: By the end of the month, the technicians will have replaced every damaged valve.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word verb phrase immediately after “technicians”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will have replaced is the spoken future perfect verb phrase.

listeningExercises.audioText: By next spring, the research assistants will have been collecting samples for eighteen months, and the study will continue.
choices: The accumulated duration of sampling up to next spring.
A single sample collected last spring.
The number of reports already published.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will have been collecting for eighteen months foregrounds duration.

listeningExercises.audioText: Please do not disturb the coordinator yet. She will be speaking to the overseas team now, if their call began on time.
listeningExercises.prompt: How certain is the coordinator’s activity?
choices: The speaker watched the call end.
The speaker is making a reasonable assumption.
The speaker has cancelled the call.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will be speaking is an inference about what is probably happening now.

listeningExercises.audioText: All the samples will have been labelled before the inspectors enter the laboratory. No unlabelled containers should remain.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is expected before the inspectors enter?
choices: The inspectors will begin labelling samples themselves.
The labels will be ordered after the visit.
Every sample will already have a label.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will have been labelled is passive future perfect describing a completed result.

listeningExercises.audioText: At eight tomorrow evening, we will be preparing the final rehearsal space.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word verb phrase immediately after “we”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will be preparing is exactly the future continuous phrase in the recording.

listeningExercises.audioText: By this September, she will have been managing the gallery for seven years.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word verb phrase immediately after “she”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will have been managing expresses duration accumulated by September.
